proof.claim:
etcd's backend file must be able to give space back, not only take it.

THE INCIDENT (2026-08-16). etcd reached its 2 GiB backend quota and raised
NOSPACE on 4 of 5 members. The control plane went read-only: no desired state
could be written, no workflow dispatched, no service registered. Recovery was
a manual compact + defrag + alarm disarm, which took the backend from 2.1 GB
to 4.2 MB.

THE WRONG DIAGNOSIS. The obvious suspect was write volume, and the controller
rewriting its whole state blob on every heartbeat looked like the culprit. An
optimization was written and shipped on that theory. It caused a second, worse
outage (see liveness-survives-state-writes) and did not stop the growth: the
backend was back to 236 MB within hours, WITH the optimization live.

THE ACTUAL CAUSE. auto-compaction was already configured — periodic, 1h
retention — so MVCC history was bounded the whole time. What was missing was
defragmentation. Compaction frees pages logically but the backend file only
ratchets upward; without a defrag the high-water mark is never returned. The
file therefore grows to whatever the busiest hour demanded and stays there
forever, and any burst that pushes one hour past the quota is permanent.

Two configuration facts made that fatal rather than merely untidy:
quota-backend-bytes was 0, meaning etcd's 2 GiB default, on a cluster whose
steady state is a few hundred MB; and nothing anywhere — no systemd timer, no
cron entry — ever ran a defrag.

THE LESSON. The measurement that settles "is this writer the problem?" is
writes-per-prefix over a window, and it was never taken. The optimization was
built on a read of the code instead. This scenario asserts the structural
property that makes write volume survivable in the first place, so the
cluster does not depend on anyone diagnosing correctly under pressure.
